literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The Booker Prize dominates the last two days, but around it there is a lovely spread of music, storytelling and writing about writing.

Let me begin with the prize. On the tenth of November, at a ceremony in London, M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything. The Los Angeles Times has the fullest account of the news. He is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner in the prize's history, and Lifestyle Asia reports that he is also the first science-fiction author to take the honour. The BBC calls the book "baffling but brilliant", which is a rather wonderful phrase to have attached to a winner. The Literary Hub report says the judges described a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile. It is an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast, so the end of the world arrives somewhere decidedly English.

If you want to understand why it won, The Observer has the main analysis piece, and that is the best place to start. Then there are the author's own words, which are the real pleasure here. In The Guardian, Harrison talks about what he calls a sci-fi alien invasion wake-up call, and says, "We are dream-walking into a desperate situation." The interview also touches on his outlook on hope and the state of the world. The New Statesman has a lighter conversation in which he admits he was "as nervous as a cat" on the night. The BBC also has a piece in which he discusses the novel himself. I only had the headline for that one, but a writer speaking about his own book is always worth a listen.

Moving from the end of the world to something gentler, there are two pieces that link music, history and fiction in just the way you enjoy. The Guardian reviews Jonathan Coe's new novel, Lessons in Harmony. It imagines a friendship between Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams, and follows their search for a musical identity. The reviewer asks what music can tell us about national identity, which is a question that sounds made for fiction. Anyone who loves classical music and likes to learn history through a novel should find this appealing, and you might even imagine a few passages for a première class on voice and place.

The Guardian also reviews The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov, the International Booker winner. It is a collection of forty stories from Bulgaria, and the reviewer praises its playful invention, its meditations on storytelling itself, and its Borgesian subversions. That suggests short pieces that wink at the reader while saying something serious, which could suit a classroom as well as a quiet evening.

On the history side, Literary Hub has a fascinating article about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. He has gone uncredited for about three centuries. Recent archival discoveries are now restoring his place in the story. It is a good tale, and a reminder of how much literary history lies hidden behind the stories we think we know.

For something different, BBC Radio 4's Open Book, broadcast on the tenth of November, features Becky Chambers talking about her new novel, As You Wake Break The Shell. It is the first book of a duology, told in alternating timelines on a planet called Fortune. She talks about the craft of building a planet from scratch, and about her Star Trek roots. Given how much you value strong characters and worlds one can step into without preparation, this one might be a good fit.

Two pieces this week are about the craft of writing itself. The Paris Review has made free its archived Art of Biography interview with Robert Caro, along with a short story by Matthew Baker called "Why Visit America". Caro on how a biography is built is a rich read for anyone who loves a well-constructed narrative. Literary Hub also has an appreciation titled The Enduring Genius of Janet Malcolm. It is written by someone who had been circling her work for years without quite realising it, and it is an essay about style and a reading life, which is a combination I think you will enjoy.

Finally, Literary Hub offers an opening excerpt called This Impossible Life, which appears to come from a novel. It is set on the outskirts of Lagos, near the Third Mainland Bridge. A character named Alohan has been dropped off by an old lady, and he wanders the roads in astonishment at his fate. The text is cut off, so I cannot say more, but the voice and the situation look promising, and it is just the sort of opening that lets you step into a place without needing to know it first.

So, to sum up: a new Booker winner with a wry smile, a Ravel and Vaughan Williams friendship, forty Bulgarian tales, and an excerpt from Lagos, plenty to pair with a cup of something warm up in Les Adrets.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The big news from the last two days is the Booker Prize, so we begin there, then wander through music and history, invented worlds, a few essays on craft, and a first page from Lagos.

The Booker Prize for 2026 was announced yesterday evening, the tenth of November, at a ceremony in London, and the winner is M. John Harrison, for a novel called The End of Everything. Several things make this a notable moment. Harrison is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest author ever to win the prize. Lifestyle Asia reports that he is also the first science-fiction author to take it, and the Los Angeles Times calls him a British science fiction writer, so the story has travelled well beyond the literary pages. The novel itself is post-apocalyptic, and the BBC's headline sums it up as "baffling but brilliant". I rather like that, because it suggests a book that does not hold your hand. Literary Hub quotes the judges describing a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile. That is a lovely combination, vertigo and a small private grin, and it tells you a good deal about the tone before you have read a page.

If you want to understand the win, the Observer has the main analysis piece, asking why Harrison's novel took the prize. I can't tell you what its argument is, since only the framing reached me, but it is the place I would start. The Guardian has an interview with Harrison under the headline "We are dream-walking into a desperate situation". It calls the novel an apocalyptic story set on the Kent coast, and describes it as his sci-fi alien invasion wake-up call. In that conversation he talks about his outlook on hope and on the state of the world. Hearing a writer of eighty-one reflect on hope, after a lifetime of imagining the end of things, seems to me worth your time. The setting is lovely in a strange way. The Kent coast is a very English edge of the world, chalk and shingle and grey water, and the idea of the end arriving there rather than in some distant desert has its own quiet unease.

There is also a lighter conversation in the New Statesman, where Harrison says he was "as nervous as a cat" on the night. After the grandeur of the headlines, it is a pleasing human detail: the oldest winner in the prize's history, and the first from science fiction, reduced to feline anxiety in a ceremony room. The BBC also has a piece in which he discusses the novel in his own words, though only the headline came through to me, so I can't promise detail. Still, a writer talking about his own book is often the best way in. And if you were looking for a conversation to have with your première pupils, a prize that has gone, for the first time, to a writer from a genre often kept at the edge of the literary table might open a good discussion about what we mean by "literary" fiction in the first place. I offer that as a thought rather than anything reported.

Now to novels that teach history and music, which I know are close to your heart. The Guardian has reviewed Jonathan Coe's Lessons in Harmony. The novel imagines a friendship between Maurice Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams, and the two composers' search for a musical identity. The reviewer's guiding question is what music can tell us about national identity. It is a rich subject, because both men were composers who looked hard at where their sounds came from, and who they were writing for. Ravel is French, of course, so he will be on your own side of the Channel, and Vaughan Williams is as English as the folk songs he gathered. A novel that sets them side by side, as friends, lets national character be explored through conversation and listening rather than lectures. That seems very much in the spirit of fiction that teaches history better than an essay can. It also sits happily beside your love of classical music, and I suspect it would send you straight back to the recordings.

From composers to a much older story. Literary Hub has an article called "How the Author of Aladdin Got Erased From History". It is about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin, and who has gone uncredited for three centuries. Recent discoveries in the archives are now restoring his place in the story. I love the shape of this one. A tale we all think of as anonymous, or as belonging to some vague and glittering Orient, turns out to have a particular man behind it, a traveller with a name, and the paper trail has only just been found. It is literary history with the pull of an adventure, and it would make a very good starter for a lesson on who gets credited with stories, and who gets left out. I don't have the detail of what the archives revealed, but the headline itself is a good teaser.

Let me move to invented worlds, which this week come in two very different sizes. On BBC Radio 4's Open Book, broadcast on the tenth of November, Becky Chambers talks about her new novel, As You Wake Break The Shell. It is the first book of a duology, told in alternating timelines on a planet called Fortune. In the conversation she talks about the business of building a planet, and about her roots in Star Trek. That second detail is rather endearing. Star Trek at its best is optimistic, curious about other beings, and fond of its characters, and I would expect a writer who grew up with it to put people at the centre of her worldbuilding. The alternating timelines are a useful device for any reader who likes to watch a narrator's knowledge unfold slowly, and I suspect the programme will have things to say about how she keeps the two threads in step. It also makes a pleasing partner to the Booker story, since you now have, in one week, two quite different ways of imagining a world: Harrison's, at the end of things, and Chambers's, at the start of a new one.

The other, smaller-scale invention comes from the Guardian, which reviews The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov. He is the Bulgarian writer who won the International Booker, and this new book is a collection of forty stories. The reviewer praises its playful invention and its meditations on storytelling, and describes its subversions as Borgesian. Borges is a good name to invoke, the writer of labyrinths, libraries and tales that fold in on themselves, and the phrase suggests stories that are aware of being stories. The title itself, a man with many names, is a lovely invitation. A collection of forty short pieces would also suit a reader who likes to dip in, a story at a time, over a few evenings. I would note that it comes from a Bulgarian writer and is reviewed in English, which is a small reminder of how much good fiction reaches us by way of translation. The review calls the book both playful and profound, which is a hard balance to strike, and it makes me curious.

Now a few pieces on the craft of writing itself, which I think you will enjoy. The Paris Review has made free its archived Art of Biography interview with Robert Caro, alongside a short story by Matthew Baker called "Why Visit America". The Paris Review's interviews are famous for taking writers seriously about the practical business of making sentences, and Caro, who has devoted his working life to the lives of powerful men, is a master of the long, patiently built narrative. I only have the framing, not the contents, but an interview about how to build a life on the page is the kind of thing that teaches you how to read narrative non-fiction, and I think it could be useful to share an extract with older pupils who are learning to structure an argument as a story. The short story is a bonus, a free piece of fiction to go with it.

Also from Literary Hub is an appreciation called "The Enduring Genius of Janet Malcolm". The writer says they had been circling her work for a long time without quite realising it. I like the honesty of that, the idea that a writer can shape your taste before you have noticed it happening. It is an essay about style and about a reading life, so it falls into that lovely category of writing about writing. If you have not read Malcolm for a while, it might prompt you to pick her up again. I can't say more about the argument than that, but the premise alone, of discovering that someone has been quietly influencing you for years, is a good one for any reader.

And to close, an opening excerpt, again from Literary Hub, called "This Impossible Life". It appears to come from a novel, and it is set on the outskirts of Lagos, by the Third Mainland Bridge. A character named Alohan has been dropped off by an old lady, and he wanders the roads in astonishment at his fate. The text we have is cut off, so I can't tell you where it goes. But the situation is a good one, a person set down in an unfamiliar place with no idea why, and it is exactly the sort of opening where a narrator's voice has to do all the work at once. It is a story you can step into without knowing the city first, which I know you value. The bridge itself, stretching over the lagoon, makes a striking image to begin on. I would treat it as a short, free taste of a possible new voice, and see whether the first paragraphs earn your trust.

So the week gives us a prize going to a writer at the far edge of his career and of the genre, a novel about two composers searching for a sound, a long-lost author of a famous tale, two inventors of worlds, and a handful of writers talking about how the work is done. Plenty to choose from for a quiet evening up in Les Adrets, and I hope one of them finds its way onto your table.

Happy reading, Yamuna, and may your next page be a good one.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news has a pleasing thread running through it: artists and their words, and paintings that seem to spill over into music, theatre and literature.

Let me begin close to home. The Musée de Grenoble is showing an exhibition on Anne Truitt called Libérer la couleur, Freeing Colour. Arts in the City carries the listing, and it gives little beyond the title, but Truitt was a sculptor whose work turns on colour, so it promises something quiet and concentrated. The museum is also building a programme around her. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from Truitt's journal, in a staging directed by Mathieu Barché. I like this idea very much: an artist's own written voice, spoken aloud in the rooms where her work hangs. It seems made for you, so it may be worth noting the dates now.

The museum also held an event on Monday the ninth, just before this briefing. For the Amis du musée, there was a screening and discussion of Caroline Champetier's 2012 film on Berthe Morisot. It has already passed, but it's a sign that the museum is thinking about how film can approach a painter's life, and perhaps it will return in some form.

From there, a thread that links painting and literature quite directly: André Malraux and his idea of the musée imaginaire. Two items from the Journal des Arts website touch on it. One is a route, a parcours, pairing Malraux with Picasso around that idea. The other is a series called L'Art est une conquête, season one, devoted to the musée imaginaire. Both texts are very short, so I can't tell you more than their titles. But Malraux was a novelist as well as a thinker about art, and the notion that we build a private museum in our heads from reproductions and memories is one that connects naturally to teaching. It might even make a good starting point for a class on how images and words feed each other.

That same idea of art overflowing its frame appears in a lovely small piece from Radio France. It asks listeners what music they can hear in Vilhelm Hammershøi's painting Paysage de Lejre. Hammershøi painted hushed, grey, almost held-breath scenes, and the question treats the landscape as something to be listened to. The article is brief, but the question is a good one to carry around with you today. Related in spirit is an exhibition at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nice called De la scène à la toile, From Stage to Canvas, which has guided visits on offer. No dates are given in the listing, so you would need to check, but the title suggests a meeting point between performance and painting. And in Paris, the Musée Gustave Moreau has handed a carte blanche to the contemporary painter Ali Banisadr, under the title Talisman. He has been invited to respond to the museum's world, and Moreau's Symbolist universe has always sat close to literature and myth. Again, the dates aren't in the text, so look at the full listing before planning anything.

Now to artists and the lives behind the work. The Guardian has a piece on Ron Howard's Netflix documentary about the photographer Richard Avedon. It recounts how Avedon said he was looking for faces that surprise him, and it includes the anecdote of the Dalai Lama laughing during a sitting. The documentary explores how Avedon tried to capture the inner self of his sitters, and it sounds like a rich study in portraiture, with the stories behind the images.

The Guardian's critic is far less kind about Tate Britain's show of Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant. The review is harsh, calling the roam through Bloomsbury flaccid, and finding the paintings less compelling than the lives, the loves and the Picasso-filled home behind them. Whether or not you agree, it raises an interesting question for anyone who loves the Bloomsbury circle: does the literary and social legend sometimes outshine the canvases? Also in The Guardian, there is a lively interview with the conceptual artist Ryan Gander. He admits to disliking painting and has little patience for the Young British Artists, whom he calls shallow and egocentric, and yet his new show is full of paintings. It's a good example of an artist contradicting himself in public, which is often where the most interesting talk happens.

For something that crosses over with your love of thrillers, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a forty-two-minute episode with Karin Slaughter. She talks about adapting her novel The Good Daughter for television, set in her native Georgia. The same programme includes a segment on a Norwich exhibition about the kiss in art, so it covers crime fiction and art history in one sitting.

Finally, two stories about history and place. Le Dauphiné Libéré is presenting an exhibition called Encordés, on the pioneers of mountaineering, past and present. The article doesn't say where or when, but with Belledonne above your house, the subject is certainly close to your world, and it may be worth a look at the paper's full piece. And 20 Minutes reports an offbeat exhibition on William the Conqueror at the château de Falaise in Normandy, taking a quirky angle on the Norman duke. The article is short, but it suggests history made tangible through objects and imagination.

That's the art for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it sends you off to look, listen or read a little more closely.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle, thoughtful day in the art world, with something close to home in Grenoble, a long conversation about Malraux and his imaginary museum, and a few sharp voices from artists and critics to keep things lively.

Let me start in Grenoble, where the Musée de Grenoble is giving its walls to Anne Truitt. The exhibition is called Libérer la couleur, Freeing Colour, and it comes via Arts in the City. The listing gives us little beyond the title, but the title says a good deal. Truitt is an artist whose work is bound up with colour, and the idea of freeing it suggests a show about colour let loose from the things it usually serves, which is rather a nice thought for a teacher of language to hold on to, since words are so often pinned to their usual meanings too.

What makes this more than a simple exhibition notice is that the museum has built a second layer around it. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from Anne Truitt's journal, directed by Mathieu Barché, at the Musée de Grenoble. Truitt was a sculptor, and so this is an artist's own written voice set beside her work, in the very rooms where the work hangs. I think that is a lovely idea. A journal is the most private kind of prose, and hearing it read aloud by an actor, with the objects themselves nearby, might tell you something no wall label could. It is a date worth putting in the diary, and the two evenings give you a little flexibility.

There was also a event at the museum just two days ago, on the ninth of November, at half past two in the afternoon. The Amis du musée screened and discussed Caroline Champetier's 2012 film on Berthe Morisot. It has already passed, so I mention it mostly as a sign of how the museum is working: it keeps pairing painters with other forms, a film here, a reading there. If you missed it, it may be worth asking the Amis du musée whether the film turns up again, or looking for it yourself, because a film that approaches a painter's life and work is exactly the kind of thing that might sit well beside a lesson on how we narrate an artist.

One more local note, though I must be honest that it is thin. Le Dauphiné Libéré is presenting an exhibition called Encordés, a title which means roped together, on the pioneers of mountaineering, past and present. The article calls it a passionate epic. The text gives no venue and no dates, so I can't tell you where to find it, but with Belledonne outside your window, the story of people tied to one another on a rock face feels like it belongs to your own horizon. A quick look at the Dauphiné's website should settle where and when.

Now to the thread that I think you'll enjoy most today, which is André Malraux and the musée imaginaire. Two items from the Journal des Arts turn on it. One is a route, a parcours, titled André Malraux et Pablo Picasso: le musée imaginaire. The other is an exhibition presented as a series, L'Art est une conquête, season one, Le Musée imaginaire. Both texts are very short, little more than titles, so I can't describe what you would actually see. But the idea is rich enough to carry a few minutes on its own. The musée imaginaire is Malraux's notion of a museum without walls, in which images of artworks from every age and place can be gathered together in the mind, and set beside one another in ways no physical building could manage. And Malraux, of course, was a novelist as well as a thinker about art, which is why pairing him with Picasso makes such sense: here is a writer asking what paintings do to us, and a painter who answered with his hands. For a teacher who likes to put a painting next to a passage of prose, the musée imaginaire is more or less your classroom method given a name. It may be worth reading the full pieces to see whether there's anything to borrow for your première classes.

Staying with the idea of art meeting another sense, Radio France has a small, charming piece asking listeners what music they hear in Vilhelm Hammershøi's painting Paysage de Lejre. Hammershøi was Danish, and this is a quiet landscape, and the question is simply: if this picture made a sound, what would it be? The text is brief, so there is no list of answers for me to share, but the question itself is a lovely classroom exercise. I could imagine you putting a quiet painting on the board and asking students to write the music rather than the description, and then seeing which adjectives surface. It's a way into poetic, musical language through the eye, and it costs nothing.

From there, let me turn to the artists who speak for themselves, because several of today's stories are about faces, voices and reputations.

The Guardian looks at Richard Avedon through Ron Howard's new Netflix documentary. The piece borrows its title from the photographer himself: I'm looking for faces which surprise me. The film traces his career and leans on anecdotes, among them the Dalai Lama laughing during a sitting. The article is about how Avedon tried to capture the inner self of the people in front of his camera, the soul as much as the likeness. For a literature teacher this is rather close to the question of narration: how do you show a character so that something unguarded slips through? A portrait and a first-person narrator are both attempts at that, and Avedon's search for surprise is a handsome way to describe it.

In a very different register, The Guardian also has an interview with the conceptual artist Ryan Gander, described as brilliantly bolshie, who lambasts practically everyone. He speaks candidly about disliking painting, and about his scorn for the Young British Artists, whom he calls shallow and egocentric, and yet his new show is full of paintings. The contradiction is the fun of it. It is a lively, provocative read, and a good reminder that artists are often their own most unreliable narrators. I would not take everything at face value, but it is the kind of voice that sticks in the memory.

And then a rather brutal review, also from The Guardian, of the Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant exhibition at Tate Britain. The critic calls it a flaccid roam through Bloomsbury's desperately mediocre modernists, which tells you where we stand. The argument is that the paintings are less compelling than the lives, the loves and the Picasso-filled home behind them. Whatever you make of that verdict, it's a useful counterpoint, because Bloomsbury is a place where painting and literature were always tangled together, and the review essentially asks whether the circle matters more than the work. It's a question you could put to students about any writer or painter whose biography is more famous than their output. You may disagree with the critic, which would make it even better material.

Away from Grenoble, a few exhibitions that I can only point to, with the usual caveats about detail.

In Paris, the Musée Gustave Moreau has given a carte blanche to the contemporary painter Ali Banisadr. The show is called Talisman, and the idea is that Banisadr responds to the world of the museum, which is the world of Moreau's Symbolist painting. Moreau's art sits very close to literature, full of myth and dreamlike scenes, so a living painter answering it is an appealing pairing. The listing gives no dates, so check the full details before planning anything, but if you are in Paris at some point this season, it sounds like a good reason to step into that museum.

In Nice, the Musée des Beaux-Arts is offering guided visits of an exhibition called De la scène à la toile, from the stage to the canvas. The title points to the link between performance and painting, which touches on your love of dance and the stage. Again, no dates are given, so it is only a pointer, but it's a theme worth following.

And in Normandy, 20 Minutes reports on an offbeat exhibition about William the Conqueror at the château de Falaise. The approach is a quirky angle on the Norman duke, and the article itself is brief. I like the idea of history coming alive through objects and a bit of humour, and Falaise is, after all, the place where the story begins. It's the sort of thing that might tempt you on a trip north, and it is a reminder that history is often best taught sideways.

Two last items stray a little from the visual arts, but both are about writing, so I'll leave them here for you.

The first is from the BBC Radio 4 programme Front Row, a forty-two minute episode in which the thriller writer Karin Slaughter talks about adapting her novel The Good Daughter for television. The story is set in her native Georgia, and she discusses what it takes to move a thriller from page to screen. The same episode also includes a segment on an exhibition in Norwich about the kiss in art, which is a pleasing change of tone. Given your fondness for thrillers, this one might make good company on a drive down the valley.

The second is a review in The Guardian of a new travelogue called With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna. The book explores queer subcultures in Budapest, Prague and other central European cities, and challenges the stereotype of the region as illiberal. The headline quotes a line that homosexuality was coined by a Hungarian. The piece touches on language, on Wittgenstein, and on an art exhibition about masculinity. It is not a book about painting, but the mix of travel writing, philosophy and the politics of words feels like it belongs on a literary reader's shelf, and I mention it for that reason.

So, in short: Anne Truitt at the Musée de Grenoble with her journal read aloud in December, Malraux's museum of the mind, a landscape that asks you what music you hear, and a handful of artists who either reveal themselves or argue with everyone. Enjoy your Wednesday, Yamuna, and may your day contain at least one surprising face.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is a gathering of what's happening around you, from this week's small outings to a rich run of evenings at the MC2 in early December.

I'll begin with the days just ahead. Today, the eleventh, is quiet, but tomorrow, Thursday the twelfth, the Jean-Renoir cinema in Pontcharra screens Au fil de l'eau. Dauphiné Libéré has the listing, though without further detail. The next evening, Friday the thirteenth of November at half past seven, the Espace Culturel Paul Jargot in Crolles stages a performance called Les enfants c'est moi. The listing says little about it, but Crolles is an easy hop down the valley from you. If you'd like ideas for the weekend, ici.fr has put together a roundup of outings across Isère for the tenth to the sixteenth of November. I only have the headline, so it may be worth a browse for yourself. There is also an Écran Total film festival at La Vence Scène in Saint-Égrève, reported by the Journal des Savoie, though I have no dates or programme, so a quick check before setting out would be wise. And yesterday, in Échirolles, there was an event called La Bande Originale de nos vies, a lovely title, although the listing doesn't say what it involved.

Now, for something slower and more contemplative, there are two free exhibitions. In Villard-Bonnot, from the seventh of November to the sixth of January, you can see work by Jean-Pierre Angei under the title Il soffio del tempo, the breath of time. The listing is brief, but it is a gentle, nearby show with a poetic title, and there's plenty of time to fit it in. Further along, at Saint-Martin-d'Hères, an exhibition runs until the third of April next year, tracing how Isère set about conquering water in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It's a piece of local history, and I thought it might interest you as a reflection on how a region tells its own past.

The biggest cluster of events comes in the first week of December, and nearly all of it is at the MC2 in Grenoble. It begins on the second, when Jean-François Sivadier's staging of Chekhov's Ivanov opens, running until the fourth. A major Russian play on stage so close to home is a real opportunity for a literature teacher, and Chekhov's weary, self-doubting hero is such a wonderful figure to watch in the flesh. On Thursday the third and Friday the fourth, there is also Mussum, a dance piece by Souhail Marchiche and Mehdi Meghari of Compagnie Dyptik. I have no more information than that, but it's contemporary dance, and a good one to keep in mind.

Friday the fourth is a busy day, because the Orchestre national de Lyon also plays that evening at the MC2, with the violinist Vilde Frang and the conductor Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider. The programme is Webern, Britten and Brahms, which sounds like a handsome piece of musical architecture, from the concentrated, glittering Webern through Britten to the warmth of Brahms at the end. A little later, on Sunday the sixth of December, the Ensemble Les Illuminations present a Sunday concert called Jouer la lumière, playing the light. I have no programme details, but a title on light feels as though it might appeal to someone who loves paintings and the way they speak to music and writing.

For something with younger audiences in mind, on the ninth of December at a quarter past two in the afternoon, Hexagone Scène nationale in Meylan presents J'étais parti·e, pardon, from Collectif Mind The Gap. It's a show about how we might change worlds, designed for ages eight and up, and lasts fifty-five minutes. There are three more dates besides that one. It might be of interest to pass on to a younger reader or a colleague with a class in mind.

And now some lighter, more rural news. France 3 Alpes reports on a sheep farm in Poisat, near Grenoble, where two shepherds have brought in a llama named Jeff to guard their flock against wolves, in place of the traditional patou dog. According to the shepherds, the flock is now calm and settled, and the headline quotes them saying the herd is calm and at peace. I rather like the idea of Jeff as a character: a quiet, watchful guardian in a story that wouldn't be out of place in a gentle fable.

Finally, a few things for the colder weeks ahead. In Chambéry, L'Essor Savoyard has published a preview of what is new at the Christmas market this year. I only have the headline, with no dates, but it's something to look out for if you fancy a December outing across the border into Savoie. And at Fontanil-Cornillon, the Salon des Vins de l'Isère is under way, a regional wine fair reported by the Journal des Savoie. Again, there are no dates, but it's the kind of producers' event that sits close to home, and worth a look if you enjoy meeting people who make what they sell.

That's the lot for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here tempts you out into the valley, even if only for Chekhov and a good cup of something warm afterwards.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Wednesday the eleventh of November, and the last couple of days have brought a pleasantly full local agenda, with plenty to look forward to in the weeks ahead and a few things happening right on your doorstep.

Let me begin with the theatre, dance and music, because December at the MC2 in Grenoble looks like a real treat. The first date to note is Wednesday the second of December. From the second to the fourth, Jean-François Sivadier stages Anton Chekhov's Ivanov. For a literature teacher, this is a rare chance to see a major Russian play on stage without leaving the valley. The listing doesn't say more about the production, so I can't tell you about casting or design, but the name of the director and the playwright together are reason enough to put it in the diary. If you ever want to bring something back to the classroom, even just the experience of a play that lives in the air of a theatre rather than on the page, three evenings give you some flexibility.

The following day, Thursday the third, and again on Friday the fourth of December, the same MC2 hosts Mussum, a dance piece by Souhail Marchiche and Mehdi Meghari of Cie Dyptik. The text gives no further detail, so I'll simply say it is contemporary dance, close to home, and that you've told us dance is a love of yours. Seeing it live is often the best way to meet a company for the first time.

Then comes Friday the fourth, which is a busy evening at the MC2. The Orchestre national de Lyon plays Webern, Britten and Brahms, with the violinist Vilde Frang and the conductor Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider. It is a strong classical programme, and a good one for a Friday evening in town. I should be honest that the listing doesn't tell us which works will be played, only the three composers. Still, that pairing of the twentieth century with Brahms promises a nicely contrasted evening. You will notice that on the fourth of December, Ivanov, Mussum and the orchestra are all happening under one roof, so it's a date where you may have a lovely dilemma. The second and third of December, and the performances of Ivanov on those days, may help you spread things out if you'd like more than one.

The MC2 has one more offering that caught my eye. On Sunday the sixth of December, the Ensemble Les Illuminations present a Sunday concert called Jouer la lumière, which means playing the light. The listing gives no further detail, but the title alone seems made for someone who thinks about painting and literature together. Light is, after all, what so many painters spend their lives pursuing, and what poets reach for too. It's a gentle way to spend a Sunday, whatever the programme turns out to be.

Moving a little to the east of Grenoble, and to something for younger audiences, though perhaps also for a curious adult. On Wednesday the ninth of December at a quarter past two in the afternoon, Hexagone Scène nationale in Meylan stages J'étais parti·e, pardon, with the subtitle "dans un autre univers". It comes from Collectif Mind The Gap and is about how we might change worlds. It is recommended for ages eight and up, runs for fifty-five minutes, and has three more dates beyond that first one. If you know a young person, or a colleague with children, it might make a nice shared outing. A Wednesday afternoon slot is also convenient when school lets out early.

Closer to the Grésivaudan, there is a live evening in Crolles very soon. On Friday the thirteenth of November, at half past seven in the evening, the Espace Culturel Paul Jargot hosts a performance called Les enfants c'est moi. The listing says nothing more than the title, so I can't describe the form or the subject, but it's a live arts evening close to Les Adrets, and that's often how a good discovery begins. A short drive down into the valley, and you're there.

Now to the visual arts, which I know you like to follow. Two free exhibitions are already open. In Villard-Bonnot, from the seventh of November until the sixth of January, there is an exhibition of work by Jean-Pierre Angei, called Il soffio del tempo, which translates as the breath of time. The listing gives little else, but I rather like the title. It has something musical about it, almost a line of poetry. With entry free and the show running right into the new year, you can go whenever it suits you, perhaps on a quiet weekend afternoon, and it is very close to home.

The other exhibition is a little further along, at Saint-Martin-d'Hères, and it's a history piece. From the nineteenth of September until the third of April, 2027, a free exhibition traces the conquest of water in Isère in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. That is a long run, so there is no rush at all. Given your interest in how the past is told and how history can come alive, it could be a good one for a grey winter afternoon. Water has shaped this region, with its mountains, its rivers and its valleys, so the subject feels very much of the place.

Now for something warmer and much more whimsical, from France 3 Alpes in Isère. It is a video report from a sheep farm in Poisat, near Grenoble, where two shepherds have brought in a llama named Jeff to protect their flock from wolves. Instead of the traditional patou, the big mountain dog, they have gone for a llama. The shepherds say the flock is now calm and settled, and the report's title quotes them: the flock is calm and at peace. It's a charming story of animals working together, and I thought it a nice change from the usual headlines about wolves. If you enjoy a good character, Jeff the llama seems to have plenty of it.

Next, the seasonal and market-type news, which grows more relevant as winter approaches. L'Essor Savoyard has a preview of what is new at the Christmas market in Chambéry for 2026. The article is a headline only as far as we can see, so I have no dates or details to give you, but it's worth keeping an eye out as December approaches. Chambéry is within easy reach, and a Christmas market is the sort of outing that is nicest when it's planned a little in advance.

In a similar spirit, for lovers of local producers, jds.fr reports that the Salon des Vins de l'Isère, the regional wine fair, is being held at Fontanil-Cornillon. Again we only have the headline, with no dates, so you'd need to check before going. But it is a producers' event close to home, which I know suits you.

And if you would like some ideas for the coming days more broadly, ici.fr has a roundup of outing suggestions across Isère for the tenth to the sixteenth of November. The text gives only the headline, so I can't pick out specifics, but it may be a useful place to look if you're planning your weekend.

Finally, cinema, which is lower on your list, but I'll mention two items briefly in case they appeal. Tomorrow, Thursday the twelfth of November, in Pontcharra, the Jean-Renoir cinema screens Au fil de l'eau, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The report gives no further detail, so I can't say what the film is about, though the title, which means something like "along the water", happens to fit nicely with the exhibition on water in Saint-Martin-d'Hères. A small coincidence, but a pleasing one. Also, jds.fr says the Écran Total film festival is taking place at La Vence Scène in Saint-Égrève. We only have the headline, with no dates or programme, so it would be worth checking the details if it tempts you.

One more item, though it has already passed. Yesterday, the tenth of November, a cultural event called La Bande Originale de nos vies took place in Échirolles. The listing is brief and I can't say anything about its content, so I'm mentioning it only so you know that it happened. The title, which means "the soundtrack of our lives", is a lovely one.

So, to gather it all together, the nearest dates are tomorrow's screening in Pontcharra and the performance in Crolles on Friday. The exhibitions at Villard-Bonnot and Saint-Martin-d'Hères can wait for a quiet afternoon. The big cluster of evenings at the MC2 begins on the second of December, and the sixth brings the Sunday concert about light. In between, the Chambéry Christmas market and the Isère wine fair are ones to watch for further details.

Wrap up warmly, Yamuna, and enjoy whichever of these catches your fancy, perhaps with a glimpse of Jeff the llama in your thoughts.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Armistice Day, and the last two days have brought a good mix of Hamlet on stage, a notable Booker win, and a few things you could take straight into class.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it's on the session twenty twenty-seven programme and has the most news. A production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief is heading to the Barbican Theatre, and new production photographs have appeared in three places: Theatre Weekly, ATV Today, and the London Evening Standard, which calls its set "exclusive first pictures". The reports are mostly picture captions, so I can't tell you much about the staging, dates or casting. Still, a new production with a distinctive title is a good prompt for a première class. You could ask pupils what a staging can change about a play they think they know, and look at the images together before reading the scenes. Hamlet also turns up in a different form. River 949 reports on Queensland Ballet's Hamlet, a dance adaptation of the play. The item is only a headline, but it's a nice thought for someone who loves both dance and Shakespeare. It raises a lovely question: what happens to a play so dense with language when the words are taken away?

Staying with the stage, tickets have gone on sale for a production of Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa in Kilcullen, according to the Kilcullen Diary. It's a local announcement without much detail, but it's another programme text being performed this season. Further afield, Our Theatre Voice reviews the Canadian premiere of Alias Grace, Margaret Atwood's novel based on a real nineteenth-century case. The reviewer praises the compelling performances and the restrained, subtle staging. It's not on the programme, but for anyone who teaches Atwood and likes to link fiction to real history, it's a fascinating companion. And one cheerful note: the Alameda Post reports that Alameda High School has staged what it calls a delightful Emma. Emma is on the oral themes list, and it's heartening to see teenagers taking on Austen with such enthusiasm.

Now to the Booker Prize, which has been the big literary story. M. John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six prize for The End of Everything. LBC reports that, at eighty-one, he's the oldest winner in the prize's history, and the first science-fiction author to take it. The Independent, on the ninth of November, called the book an apocalypse novel, and LBC describes it as dystopian. Those pieces are news reports rather than readings of the book, so I can't say much about the novel itself. But it's a late-career triumph, and a good reminder of how far the prize has widened. If your students are working on dystopian fiction for the oral, the win gives you a timely hook about what counts as literary fiction today.

That connects neatly to dystopia, which has a few items this morning. The Boar, a student paper, asks why we are so obsessed with dystopia, and describes the genre as a mix of triumph and hopelessness. That phrase alone is useful. It could frame a discussion across The Handmaid's Tale, Nineteen Eighty-Four and The Road: do these books leave us despairing, or somehow braced? Related to this, The University Times reports that the Irish novelist Paul Lynch is to visit The Phil. Prophet Song is one of the oral themes, and although I don't have a date, it's worth noting, since an author's own voice, in an interview or talk, can bring a book to life for students. Hotpress also reports that Margaret Atwood, Sebastian Barry and Louise Kennedy are on the lineup for the Festival of Writing and Ideas in twenty twenty-seven. Again, it's only a headline, so there are no dates or venue. But Atwood's presence, and that of an Irish writer as distinguished as Sebastian Barry, make it one to keep an eye on.

Finally, two pieces that could go straight into lessons. The Washington Post, published on Armistice Day, traces how John McCrae's In Flanders Fields began as a patriotic poem and became an anti-war anthem. It's a splendid case study in how a text's meaning shifts over time. It sits nicely alongside history and war poetry, and it would make a good starting point for asking pupils how readers, rather than writers, change what a poem means. If you're thinking about the Blake on the twenty twenty-seven programme, Britannica has a clear piece on how The Lamb and The Tyger work as contrasting symbols. It's a straightforward take on innocence and experience, probably most useful for seconde or première, and could serve as a neat starting handout before pupils do their own close reading. A tip would be to ask them to read both poems aloud, because Blake's music is half the argument.

So, to sum up: Hamlet is having a busy week in London and in Queensland, the Booker has gone to a science-fiction writer for the first time, and Armistice Day brings a fine example of how poems change meaning over time. I hope the day treats you kindly up in Les Adrets.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Armistice Day, and the last two days have been a good mix of poetry, Hamlet in performance, a notable Booker win and a few small stage items that touch the programme.

Let me begin with the poems, since today invites it. The Washington Post has published a piece for Armistice Day on how John McCrae's "In Flanders Fields" began as a patriotic poem and became an anti-war anthem. I only have the outline of the article, not the full text, but the question it raises is a lovely one for a classroom: can the meaning of a poem change without a single word of it changing? The answer seems to be that the world around the poem changes, and the poem is read differently as a result. This works well with première students, who are often ready to think about a text's afterlife as well as its first intentions. You might put the poem in front of them with no context, ask what it seems to want from its reader, and then give them the history of how it has been used. The gap between those two readings is where the discussion lives. It would also sit well beside any of the war poetry you already use, and, thinking ahead to the 2028 session, it is a quiet companion to The Return of the Soldier.

Staying with poetry, Britannica has an explainer on how "The Lamb" and "The Tyger" work as contrasting symbols in Blake. It is a clear, classroom-ready piece, and Songs of Innocence and of Experience is on the 2027 programme. I wouldn't call it a deep critical reading, but for seconde or an early première lesson it offers a clean way in. The two poems are a natural pair: one creature gentle, one fearsome, and the same maker behind both. A simple exercise would be to give students the two poems on one sheet and ask them to list what each speaker asks and what each speaker seems to know. The questions in "The Tyger" are famously unanswered, and watching students notice that is always a pleasure. If you want to follow the Armistice thread, you could ask the same question of Blake and of McCrae: who is speaking, and who are they speaking for?

Now to Hamlet, which is having a busy few days. Three outlets, Theatre Weekly, ATV Today and the London Evening Standard, have all published new production photographs of a staging titled Hamlet Hail to the Thief, at the Barbican Theatre in London. The Evening Standard calls its pictures exclusive first photographs. I should be honest that the coverage I have is thin: no dates, no cast, no word on the director's approach. So I can't tell you what the production is doing with the play. What I can say is that Hamlet is on the 2027 list, and a major London staging with fresh images in circulation is the kind of thing that makes a stage version easy to bring into the room. Even without a recording, production photographs are useful. You could show students a single image and ask what it tells them about the production's reading of the play, before they've been told anything. Costume, lighting, the space around the actor: students are often better readers of a stage picture than they expect. It would be worth keeping an eye out for reviews once the production opens, as those would give you far more to work with.

Hamlet also turns up in a different art form. River 949 has a headline about Queensland Ballet's production of Hamlet, a dance adaptation of the play. Again, I only have the headline, so I can't describe the choreography or the casting. But I thought of you straight away, given your love of dance documentaries and the fact that Hamlet is a 2027 text. A ballet Hamlet raises a fascinating question for students: what survives when you take away the words? The play is so much about language, about speech and silence and the gap between what is said and what is meant. How do you dance a soliloquy? Even as a thought experiment, with no footage, it could be a lively way to get students thinking about what is essential in the play. You could ask them to choose three moments they would insist on keeping in a wordless version, and to justify each one.

Let me turn now to the Booker Prize, which was announced in the last couple of days. M. John Harrison has won with The End of Everything. The Independent, writing on the ninth of November, says that at eighty-one he is the oldest winner in the prize's history, and calls the book an apocalypse novel. LBC adds that he is the first science-fiction author to win, and describes the book as dystopian. KSAT carried the news as well, though I only have its headline. These are news reports rather than readings of the novel, so I can't tell you much about the book itself. But the milestones are striking. A prize that has long been associated with a certain kind of literary fiction has now gone to a writer from science fiction, and to the oldest author it has ever honoured. For a teacher, that is a nice prompt about how genre boundaries move. Students often assume that "literary" and "genre" are fixed categories, and a headline like this invites them to ask who decides, and why that line might be softening. It also connects neatly to your oral themes, where dystopian and speculative works already sit comfortably next to Austen and Hartley.

And that leads to a student-paper piece worth a mention. The Boar, a student newspaper, asks why we are so obsessed with dystopia, pointing to the odd mix of triumph and hopelessness in these stories. It is a student piece rather than an academic one, but the question is a good one and maps directly onto the oral list: The Handmaid's Tale, 1984, The Road, and, if you count it, Never Let Me Go, Parable of the Sower and Prophet Song. You could use the question as a warm-up for an oral preparation session. Why do readers keep returning to these worlds? What do they get from them? And is there a difference between a dystopia that ends in defeat and one that leaves a window open? Having students argue that out loud is good oral practice in itself.

Margaret Atwood appears twice in today's news. First, Our Theatre Voice has reviewed the Canadian premiere of Alias Grace, the stage version of her novel, which is based on a real nineteenth-century case. The reviewer praises the compelling performances and what they call restrained, subtle staging. I don't have details of the adaptation beyond that, and Alias Grace isn't itself on your programme, but it speaks to something you like: fiction rooted in real history, where a story teaches the past in a way a textbook can't. For students of The Handmaid's Tale, it is a useful reminder that Atwood is a writer who keeps returning to women's testimony and to how stories get told about them. The phrase "restrained, subtle staging" is also worth noting. It suggests that a story with a lot of dramatic potential can be told quietly, which is a good thing to discuss when students compare novel and stage adaptation.

Second, Hotpress reports that Atwood is on the lineup for the Festival of Writing and Ideas in 2027, alongside Sebastian Barry and Louise Kennedy. The text is only a headline, so there are no dates or venue, and I wouldn't plan anything around it yet. But it is a good sign for the year ahead, and it may be worth a look once more detail appears, especially if any sessions are recorded or streamed for a wider audience.

On the subject of authors, The University Times reports that the Irish novelist Paul Lynch is to visit The Phil, the student society at Trinity College Dublin. Prophet Song is one of your oral themes, so this is worth noting. I don't have a date for the visit, but visits like this often produce talks or interviews that end up online, and an author speaking about his own book is a wonderful thing to bring into an oral preparation session. Keep an ear out for anything recorded. Hearing a novelist explain why he wrote a dystopia set in a recognisable, contemporary Ireland, rather than in some distant future, would give students a vivid way into the book's method.

Finally, two small items about stages, one in California and one in Ireland. The Alameda Post reports that Alameda High School has staged what it calls a delightful production of Emma. It is on your oral list, and I like the item simply as good news: young people taking on Austen and, by the sound of it, enjoying themselves. If your students are working on Emma, it might be a pleasing thing to mention, a reminder that these novels are lived in as well as studied. You could even ask your students how they would stage the book's famously comic misreadings, and what a drama version gains and loses by not having Austen's narrator to guide it.

And in Kilcullen, the local Kilcullen Diary announces that tickets are on sale for a production of Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa, which is on the 2027 programme. It is a local announcement with very little detail beyond that, so I can't tell you who is staging it or when. But it is a good reminder that Friel's play, with its sisters, its music and its dancing, lives on community stages as well as professional ones. If any of your students have a connection to amateur or school theatre, it is a nice way to show that the programme isn't just a list of set texts but a repertoire people still choose to perform.

So, to gather the threads: a poem whose meaning moved, a Blake pairing ready for the classroom, Hamlet in photographs and in dance, a Booker win that widens the field, and Atwood and Lynch keeping the dystopian oral themes in the news. Nothing here that needs doing today, but plenty to think about over a cup of tea with the mountains behind you, and I hope the day is a gentle one.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Armistice Day, so today's French news begins with memory, then moves through the classroom, the Alps and a quiet film for the evening.

At the ceremony this morning, Emmanuel Macron paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau and to the Unknown Soldier. Franceinfo notes that it is his last Armistice ceremony as head of state, and that this year the emphasis falls on Marshal Foch.

That fits nicely with a piece, also from franceinfo, that rebuilds the last days and hours before the signing at Compiègne in nineteen eighteen. It draws on the writings of Captain Paul Laperche, the interpreter who was in the room when the armistice was signed in Foch's railway carriage. It's history told by a witness, which you may find more vivid than any textbook.

On a gentler note, franceinfo visited the Collège du Vieux Chêne in Chessy, in Seine-et-Marne, where pupils marked the day with readings from soldiers' letters and a song. They were speaking for themselves for the first time, and one of them said it was more interesting than a lesson. And if you're stopping at a market this morning, The Local has a small word of the day that suits the occasion: bleuet, the cornflower, which the piece links to one of two French flowers associated with public holidays.

On the practical side, today is a public holiday, and franceinfo has a guide to what is open. Most hypermarkets are open, while most banks, hairdressers and estate agencies are shut. So a baker's or a market stall is a safer bet than a bank, whether you're in Grenoble or nearer home.

Now to schools, where there is a lot of news, and some of it bears directly on your seconde and première classes. The pupil protests continue to ripple through the system. The education minister, Edouard Geffray, has again refused to move the dates of the baccalauréat. Sébastien Lecornu was set to meet lycée and student representatives on Monday afternoon. Franceinfo also reports that the government is ruling out a postponement for now, even though some programmes have fallen behind because of the disruption. Instead it is proposing extra support classes. The debate over whether the bac should be adapted, perhaps with a lighter syllabus or changes to the exams, is clearly not over.

There is a human cost on the other side too. A headteachers' union says about fifty heads have asked to be transferred after the protests, describing colleagues as discouraged and even traumatised. Some are moving to collèges, some are leaving the profession altogether, and sick leave is rising. It's a sobering reminder of how much school leadership depends on the people doing it.

Another story will matter to anyone who works in a lycée. In Brest, two plainclothes police officers collected the names, first names and photos of nearly four and a half thousand pupils from three lycées on the fourth of November, under a judicial requisition. Parents, pupils and unions are calling it "fichage", which means the gathering of data on pupils, and they are objecting strongly.

There is also a report for the Élysée from the commission on generative AI and vulnerabilities. Its co-chair, Amine Benyamina, warns of a "cognitive debt" and an "emotional debt", saying that the use of AI can alter the way people think, reflect and make decisions. You will probably have your own views on what that means for essays and close reading.

Staying with language, The Local has two items this week. The word of the day is chouchouter, the verb that grows out of chouchou, meaning a favourite or a term of endearment, and the article explains its several uses. The expression of the day is avoir les codes. I only have a short teaser for that one, but it's a handy idiom to keep for a class.

On to history. Five harki families have lodged a complaint about how their relatives' remains were handled in the nineteen sixties at the Saint-Maurice-l'Ardoise camp, in the Gard. They want to know the truth about the children who died there. It's a painful chapter of French history coming back into view, and on a day devoted to remembrance it seems worth noting.

Closer to home, a report published on Tuesday called for stronger cooperation between France and Switzerland on managing water around Geneva, the Ain and Haute-Savoie. The argument is that floods and droughts, in the report's words, "don't care about human borders". It's about the neighbouring Alps rather than Belledonne, but the same pressures reach the whole region.

And for an evening when you might want something quiet, The Guardian reviews Whispers in the Woods, Vincent Munier's French nature documentary, filmed in the Vosges. It follows a father and son as they look for lynx, foxes and deer. The reviewer describes it as tender, visually stylised and emotionally driven, with scenes such as paddling in the moonlight, rather than in the manner of Attenborough. It sounds like a film that takes its time and rewards patience.

That's the news for today, Yamuna, and I hope the holiday gives you a little time for a cornflower, a good book and a slow cup of something warm.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Wednesday the eleventh of November, a public holiday in France, so today's briefing begins with memory and language, moves through a busy week in the schools, and ends with a film, a river valley and a practical note about what's open.

Let's start with Armistice Day itself. Franceinfo has a piece that takes you through the eleventh of November, nineteen eighteen, day by day and almost hour by hour, towards the signing of the armistice at Compiègne. The signing took place in Marshal Foch's railway carriage, and the account is built from the writings of Captain Paul Laperche, the interpreter who was in the room. It's a lovely example of history told through a single witness, the sort of firsthand voice that you often say can teach more than a textbook chapter. A man whose job is to carry words between two sides, standing in a railway carriage while a war ends: there is something almost novelistic about it, and it would sit very well beside the war poetry and letters you might use in class.

In Paris this morning, Emmanuel Macron presided over the ceremony. Franceinfo reports that he paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau and to the Unknown Soldier, and that this is his last Armistice ceremony as head of state. This year the emphasis falls on Marshal Foch, which ties in neatly with the story of the railway carriage.

A gentler echo of all this comes from Seine-et-Marne, east of Paris. At the Collège du Vieux Chêne in Chessy, pupils marked the day with readings from soldiers' letters and a song, and franceinfo says it was the first time they had spoken for themselves at the commemoration. One pupil is quoted saying it is "more interesting than during a lesson", which I suspect every teacher will recognise with a smile, and perhaps a small sigh. There is something moving about teenagers reading the actual words of young men not much older than themselves, from a century ago. The letters do the teaching, and the pupils simply give them a voice.

Staying with the day, The Local France has a few small language items that fit it nicely. The first is the French word of the day, bleuet, which means the cornflower. The Local links it to Armistice Day, noting that it is one of two French flowers associated with public holidays. It's a short, light piece, and a good one to have in your pocket, because a single flower can carry a great deal of meaning once you know the story behind it.

The Local's other offerings are about how French is actually used. The word of the day is chouchouter, a verb that comes from chouchou, meaning a favourite, or a term of endearment. The article goes through its several uses, and it is a pleasing word to say aloud: to pamper, to treat someone as your favourite. And the expression of the day is avoir les codes, which translates literally as "to have the codes". The text I have is only a short teaser, so I can't tell you more about how The Local explains it, but it's the kind of idiom that rewards a moment's thought about how a language packs a whole social idea into a few ordinary words.

Now to the schools, where it has been a heavy few days. For some weeks, lycée pupils across France have been mobilising, and the question now is what it means for the baccalauréat. Franceinfo reports that the government is ruling out postponing the exams for now, even though there have been delays in covering the programmes during the protests. Instead, it is proposing extra classes. The education minister, Edouard Geffray, has again refused to change the dates of the bac, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was due to meet representatives of lycée and university students on Monday afternoon. Franceinfo also looks at the wider debate, which includes support lessons, lighter programmes and possible changes to the papers themselves, and asks whether the bac should be adapted at all. I'll keep clear of the political arguments, but for a teacher of seconde and première the practical question is a real one: how much of the programme will be covered, and how. It may be worth keeping an eye on what your own school says in the coming days.

There is also a human cost on the other side of the staffroom door. A headteachers' union says that about fifty heads of schools have asked to be transferred after the pupil protests. The union describes colleagues as discouraged and even traumatised. Franceinfo reports that some are moving to collèges, some are leaving the profession altogether, and sick leave is rising. It is a sobering reminder that when a school year becomes difficult, the people holding it together feel the strain too.

A different story with a school setting comes from Brest, in Brittany. On the fourth of November, two plainclothes police officers collected the names, first names and photographs of nearly four and a half thousand pupils from three lycées, acting under a judicial requisition. Parents, pupils and unions have denounced this as "fichage", which means the compiling of files on people. Franceinfo's report is about the unease it has caused. I only have the outline of the story, not the reasons behind the requisition, so I would not draw conclusions from it. But as a lycée teacher, you will see why the question of who holds pupils' photographs and names, and why, matters.

And one more education story, this time about technology. The commission on generative AI and vulnerabilities has presented its report to the Élysée. Those are striking phrases. Cognitive debt in particular sounds like something that builds up quietly, the way a loan does, when one hands over the effort of thinking. For anyone who teaches students to read closely and write in their own voice, it will feel very close to home. I don't have the commission's recommendations to hand, only the warning, but it is a conversation worth following.

Let me turn to history of a more painful kind. Five harki families have lodged a complaint over how their relatives' remains were handled in the nineteen sixties, at the Saint-Maurice-l'Ardoise camp in the Gard. Franceinfo reports that they want the truth, in particular about the children who died there. The harkis were the Algerians who fought alongside the French army, and the camps are part of a chapter of French history that has often been left in the shadows. This is the kind of subject that novels and testimonies sometimes reach before official history does, and it is a reminder that the past is still being asked questions, and still being answered slowly.

What sets it apart, according to the review, is its approach: quiet, driven by emotion rather than information, and visually stylised, quite unlike the Attenborough style of natural history. It sounds like the kind of film in which patience and stillness are the whole point, closer to poetry than to a lecture, and it might suit a slow evening by the fire in Les Adrets.

On Tuesday, an official report called for stronger cooperation between France and Switzerland on water management, around Geneva, the Ain and Haute-Savoie. The Local France quotes the argument that floods and droughts "don't care about human borders". It's a simple phrase, and a good one. Otherwise, it is a day well suited to a walk, a book, and a thought for Captain Laperche in his railway carriage.

That's the news for today, Yamuna. I hope your holiday is as slow and as kind as the best of those moonlit woods.

Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news runs from a very late literary triumph to glowworms in a garden shed, with a few lovely surprises in between.

Let me start with books, since the biggest story is yours. M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, announced at a ceremony in London. At eighty-one, he becomes the oldest author ever to win, and according to Lifestyle Asia, the first science-fiction author to take the prize. The BBC calls the novel "baffling but brilliant", which is a rather wonderful thing to have on your cover. The judges, quoted by Literary Hub, describe a book that turns you upside down and still raises a wry smile. It is an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast, and The Observer has a good analysis of why it won, if you want a place to begin.

The author interviews are the most fun. In The Guardian, Harrison talks about hope and the state of the world, and says that "we are dream-walking into a desperate situation", which he ties to the wake-up call of an alien invasion story. Then in the New Statesman he admits that on the night he was "as nervous as a cat". It is a pleasing mix of grim vision and very human nerves, and it makes me want to hear him read aloud.

Staying with stories, Literary Hub has a piece on Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. He has gone uncredited for about three centuries, but recent archival discoveries are putting him back into the story. It is literary history with the pull of a good tale, and it might make a lovely starting point for a class on who gets remembered as an author, and who doesn't.

Another discovery, a more accidental one. Upworthy reports that a PhD student in archaeology stumbled on a lost Maya city while searching on Google, reportedly on page sixteen of the results. That is further down than most of us ever scroll, so patience seems to have been rewarded.

Now to the stage and the dance floor. Peter Marinker, now eighty-five, is carrying on his stage career despite a diagnosis of Alzheimer's. Positive News says he is taking the role in Samuel Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape, a play about an old man listening to the recorded voice of his younger self.
