Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a bookish streak, with a surprising literary prize, a few stories about stories, and then some quieter, more hopeful news from the natural world and from people looking after one another.

Let me start with the Booker Prize, because it was announced this week and it is a lovely one. The 2026 prize has gone to M. John Harrison, for a novel called The End of Everything. The BBC reports it under the headline calling the book "baffling but brilliant", which I rather like as a verdict on a prize winner. The book is post-apocalyptic, and The Guardian describes it as an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast. Literary Hub reports that the winner was announced at a ceremony in London, and that the judges describe a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile. That is an unusual combination, being turned upside down and left smiling, and it makes me curious about the book's tone.

There are two milestones attached to the win. Lifestyle Asia reports that Harrison becomes the first science-fiction author to take the prize. The Guardian adds that at eighty-one he is the oldest author ever to win it. I find both rather cheering. The first is a small crack in an old wall between so-called literary fiction and the fiction of strange worlds, a wall that many readers, and I suspect many of your students, have never quite believed in anyway. The second is a reminder that a writing life can bear its most visible fruit very late.

If you would like to read more, the pieces have different flavours. The Observer has the main analysis, explaining why this novel won, and that is the best place to start if you want the argument for the book. The Guardian has an interview in which Harrison talks about hope and the state of the world. He describes us as dream-walking into a desperate situation, and he calls the book a sort of wake-up call, set against the idea of an alien invasion. It is a bleak phrase, but it comes from a writer who has just been given one of the great honours in English-language fiction, so there is an interesting tension there. And the New Statesman has a gentler conversation in which Harrison admits he was, in his own words, "as nervous as a cat" on the night. I like that very much. An eighty-one-year-old author with a long career behind him, still nervous as a cat, is the kind of detail that makes a writer feel like a person rather than a monument. It might even be a nice thing to share with a class who think great authors are born serene.

From one prize to a much older story, and a literary mystery with a good ending. Literary Hub has a piece on Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. For some three centuries he has gone uncredited. The good news is that recent archival discoveries are now restoring his place in the story. I think this is the kind of tale you enjoy, because it is about how a story travels, and about who gets remembered and who gets quietly erased along the way. Aladdin is one of those tales that feels as though it has always existed, as though it floated up out of the air. The notion that a real man, with a real and adventurous life, lies somewhere behind it makes the tale feel more human. It also gives a tidy example of the idea that stories are made by people, and that justice, even very late justice, is sometimes possible.

There is a companion story in the same spirit from the world of archaeology. Upworthy reports that a PhD student stumbled upon a lost Maya city while searching on Google, reportedly on page sixteen of the search results. Most of us give up around page two, so that is a fine argument for persistence, or perhaps for idle curiosity. It is a charming reminder that the past is not entirely finished with us, and that discovery sometimes comes from looking in a place where nobody thought to look.

Now to two stories about performance, presence and ageing, which I think you will enjoy. The first is a documentary, and it is on your ARTE platform. It is called Lindy hop: se déconnecter et se rencontrer, part of the ARTE Regards series. It runs for thirty-one minutes, it was made in Germany, and it will be available until the ninth of November, twenty twenty-seven, so there is no rush. It follows people who turn away from their screens and towards lindy hop, in Paris, in Pisa, and at Herräng in Sweden. It is described as a warm, human portrait of dance as a way back to presence. I like the idea of it. Lindy hop is a dance of partnership, of small improvisations, and of music that makes it hard to stay sitting down. A half-hour film about people finding one another through it sounds like the right length for a quiet evening, perhaps with the same pleasure you take in dance documentaries more generally.

The second story is from the stage. Positive News reports on Peter Marinker, now eighty-five, who is continuing his acting career after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. He has taken a role in Samuel Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape. The report is brief, so I will not pretend to know more than that. But I think the choice of play is quietly striking. Krapp's Last Tape is a play about an old man listening to recordings of his younger self, and about memory, time and what remains. For an actor living with Alzheimer's to take it on is brave, and to carry on working at all is a kind of defiance. It is a good story to set beside the Booker news, in fact. Harrison at eighty-one and Marinker at eighty-five, both showing that creative life does not have to politely retire at a certain age.

Let me turn now to nature, where this week brings three stories of real, measurable recovery. I find these particularly good to tell, because they are not promises, they are things that have already happened.

The first is the smallest and perhaps the most enchanting. Good News Network reports that a volunteer called Peter Cooper breeds glowworms in his garden shed, and releases the larvae into a nature reserve in North Yorkshire. The insects had not been seen there for a hundred years. Now, thanks to him, they shine there again. I love the picture of it, a man in a shed, patiently rearing tiny creatures that make their own light, and doing it for no payment at all. The report says the larvae were reared pro bono, which is a rather grand phrase for a very humble and loving piece of work. A century is a long time for a place to go dark, and he has quietly switched the lights back on.

The second comes from the far side of the world and is a good deal grander. Good News Network reports that Chile's Atacama Desert, recently the driest place on Earth, has burst into an exceptional bloom. Some two hundred species are flowering, and a few of them in places that had not been seen in bloom since before the millennium. What makes the story so striking is where the flowers came from. They came from seeds and tubers that had been waiting underground, sometimes for years, simply holding on until the right conditions arrived. It is hard not to think of this as a kind of parable, and the poet in you may enjoy the image of a whole landscape of patience, dormant and then suddenly vivid. The word that comes to mind is waiting, and what waiting can turn into.

The third is a conservation success in Scotland. Good News Network reports that ten years after Scotland banned industrial scallop dredging, the maerl beds of the Summer Isles are recovering, and fish stocks there are thriving. Maerl is a pink seaweed that grows in a hard, coral-like form and forms beds on the seabed, and those beds appear to be doing what a healthy habitat should, supporting more life. What I find most appealing is that the islanders themselves credit their own protection work for the change. So this is not only a story about a law, but about people who stayed and cared for a stretch of sea they lived beside. The Summer Isles is a beautiful setting, and it is good to have a story where a ban, a decade of patience and a community all line up to produce a clear result.

Finally, two stories about people, both small in scale and large in heart.

The Optimist Daily has a profile of Prince Bashangezi, as part of its Local Changemakers series for twenty twenty-six. He was an A-Level student at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, and when the COVID lockdowns took away his schooling, he felt the loss personally. Rather than leave it there, he turned that loss into peer tutoring for other refugee students. I think this will resonate with you as a teacher. It is a clear and simple example of education passed hand to hand, from one student to another, in circumstances where nobody would have blamed him for simply waiting for things to improve. He made them improve for others, and that seems to me to be teaching at its most basic and most generous.

The last story is the sweetest, and it comes from Upworthy. A birth mother phoned an adoption agency to turn down an out-of-state adoption. She expected to leave a brief refusal and be done with it. Instead, she reached an answering machine, and the greeting she heard was unscripted and joyful. And that greeting changed her mind. There is something very novelistic about the turning point being so small and so human, a few warm words on a recording, and not a grand speech or a long argument. It is the sort of moment a good writer would make a whole chapter pivot on. And it is a gentle reminder that kindness, even unplanned kindness, can reach someone at exactly the moment she needs it.

So that is the news today, from a Booker winner who was nervous as a cat to a desert full of flowers, and I hope there is something in it to carry with you into your afternoon in Les Adrets.

And a story of literary detection from Literary Hub. It's about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin, and who has gone uncredited for three centuries. Recent archival discoveries are putting him back into the story, and it's a good tale about who gets to be remembered as the author of a tale.

On the stage, there's some good news from Positive News. Peter Marinker, now eighty-five, is carrying on with his career after an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and is taking a role in Samuel Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape. The report is brief, but a veteran actor returning to Beckett, a play all about memory, feels quietly remarkable.

On to art, and something close to home. The Musée de Grenoble is showing an exhibition on Anne Truitt, called Libérer la couleur, or Freeing Colour. Arts in the City tells us little more than the title, but it's a local show about an artist whose work centres on colour, so it could be a nice outing. On the radio, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a forty-two-minute episode with the thriller writer Karin Slaughter. She talks about adapting her novel The Good Daughter for television, set in her native Georgia. The same programme has a segment on a Norwich exhibition about the kiss in art, so it brings together thrillers and painting.

If you'd like something to watch with your coffee, the Royal Ballet and Opera have put two excerpts from Kenneth MacMillan's Requiem on YouTube. The ballet is set to Fauré and was made as an elegy for John Cranko, and it was created for Stuttgart Ballet after his death. One clip is the "Libera me", a meditation on grief and consolation. The other is the "Sanctus", a luminous ensemble piece, heavy with grief. Together they'd make a quiet start to the day, or a good way to end it.

Closer to Les Adrets now. France 3 Alpes has a charming story from a sheep farm in Poisat, near Grenoble. Two shepherds have brought in a llama named Jeff to guard their flock against wolves, instead of a traditional patou dog. They say the flock is now calm and settled, and I rather hope somebody puts Jeff in a children's book. And L'Essor Savoyard has a preview of what's new at this year's Christmas market in Chambéry. There are no dates or details yet, but it's worth keeping an eye on for a December outing.

Last of all, some good news from the Good News Network. Chile's Atacama Desert, recently the driest place on Earth, has burst into an exceptional bloom, with around two hundred species in flower. A few are blooming in places where nobody has seen them flower since before the millennium. The seeds and tubers were simply waiting underground, which feels like a lesson for a Wednesday in November.

That's your briefing, Yamuna. I hope your day is full of good sentences and a little unexpected colour.
